title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes — Non‑informative Result under Shared‑Generation Semantics
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) that tested whether a deterministic verifier pipeline (generate → deterministic_netops_validator_v5 → optional repair) reduces verifier‑detected unsafe intent→configuration proposals from a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 preregistered intent→configuration tasks in a paired design comparing baseline LLM‑only and a guarded pipeline (gpt-5-mini + deterministic validator). Execution used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one LLM call per task) to conserve model budget, producing model_calls_used = 200. Outcome (adversarial cluster): baseline SAFE = 200/200; guarded SAFE = 200/200 (paired contingency n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0). Paired SAFE‑rate difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and the observed baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis (that the deterministic verifier reduces unsafe proposals) was not testable in this execution. We publish the complete preregistered run and artifacts, provide an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of testability failure, and give concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, and exploratory ROC reserves) for informative repeats. All execution and analysis artifacts cited below are archived in the supplied bundle.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→device‑configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) promises operational efficiency for NetOps but raises acute safety concerns: misordered or constraint‑violating changes can cause outages or policy breaches. A common mitigation is tool‑augmentation—pairing generation with deterministic validators, sandboxed replay, or constrained executors in generate–validate–repair pipelines—yet the causal impact of such augmentation under adversarial prompts is underexplored in reproducible, preregistered NetOps evaluations.

We preregistered (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) and executed a paired confirmatory study to estimate whether a deterministic verifier reduces the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe proposals from a hosted LLM on synthetic NetOps tasks. The preregistered estimand was the paired difference in unsafe‑proposal rate (guarded − baseline), tested with an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CIs (10000 resamples, seed 1729). Key resources for the run (task generator, validator, model configuration, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts) are archived in the bundle.

Contributions. (1) A complete, deterministic preregistered paired run (N=200) comparing baseline LLM generation and a guarded validator pipeline with archived artifacts and deterministic reconciliation. (2) An artifact‑grounded diagnosis showing why the executed run was non‑informative for the preregistered causal estimand (shared generation semantics + validator labeled all candidates SAFE + no repairs applied). (3) Concrete, artifact‑supported design recommendations to make future repeats informative (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration using the reserved exploratory items, pilot checks, and repair instrumentation). We emphasize that the observed ceiling outcome is a testability/failure‑of‑design result—not evidence that the pipeline guarantees safety in production.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and prototypes document rapid interest in LLMs for NetOps tasks (intent translation, configuration synthesis, diagnosis) while flagging safety and evaluation challenges [1,2,3]. A recurring pattern is tool‑augmentation—coupling LLMs with deterministic validators or simulators in generate–validate–repair or divide–verify–refine pipelines—which empirical studies show can reduce explicit constraint violations on curated tasks when the external verifier captures relevant domain constraints [6,2].

Work on guardrails, schema‑based tool interfaces, and secure orchestration emphasizes practical trade‑offs: stricter validators can lower acceptance of unsafe proposals but may increase false refusals and operator burden; red‑team studies in adjacent domains show guardrails must be stress‑tested with adversarial templates and ROC‑style diagnostics where feasible [4,7]. Evaluation methodology literature for agentic NetOps argues for workflow‑centred, replayable, sandboxed experiments with explicit initial/final states and archived verifier traces to permit reproducible auditing [5].

Our study aligns with these themes by using a deterministic task generator, sandboxed deterministic validation, a preregistered paired estimand, and archived validator traces; it addresses the gap of reproducible, preregistered adversarial NetOps experiments that quantify the paired causal effect of adding a deterministic verifier under controlled generation semantics.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study preregistration (cand-2026-01-prereg-v1) predefined the primary estimand as paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (guarded − baseline) on binary SAFE indicators produced by a deterministic sandbox validator. Confirmatory test: exact two‑sided McNemar; CIs: paired bootstrap percentile (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). Planned paired episodes: 200 tasks × 2 arms = 400 episodes; planned maximum_model_calls for independent per‑arm generation = 400.

Task generation and scope. A deterministic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks constrained to IPv4 reachability and limited fields (admin, mtu, vlan). Each task manifest includes initial_state, expected_final_state, explicit workflow policies (required_sequence), difficulty metadata, and a per‑task generation_seed. Tasks were partitioned into benign and adversarial clusters by preregistered adversarial transform templates; an exploratory reserve of up to 50 tasks was preregistered to calibrate adversarial strength before the confirmatory execution.

Pipelines and generation semantics. Baseline pipeline: LLM candidate accepted and scored post hoc by deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Guarded pipeline: validate the candidate in a deterministic sandbox; repairs could be invoked once per task per preregistration, but in this confirmatory run repair_provider_trace entries are null (no repairs applied). The preregistration allowed two generation semantics: (A) independent per‑arm generation (one LLM call per arm per task) or (B) shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per task whose candidate is scored by both arms). The executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false) to conserve hosted model budget.

Model, budget, and seeds. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). Executed model_calls_used = 200 (one LLM call per task). Bootstrap parameters: resamples = 10000, seed = 1729. All RNGs and generator seeds used in task production were preregistered and archived.

Scoring and analysis. The deterministic validator applied full_intent_constraint_validation and emitted validator.valid (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE) plus structured violation lists (validation_before/after). Confirmatory binary outcomes derive from validator.valid. Analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1 to produce the 2×2 contingency (n11,n10,n01,n00), exact McNemar p‑value, and paired bootstrap CIs. Preregistered missingness/exclusion/retry rules were applied (one automatic retry for failed model calls; contaminated or nondeterministic tasks excluded and replaced). Deterministic reconciliation and provider audits were recorded and archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The execution manifest records completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired episodes), failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 200, consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics and no technical failures or exclusions. Provider audit notes hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and cache_miss_count = 200.

Primary confirmatory outcomes. The deterministic validator labeled every confirmatory episode SAFE: baseline SAFE successes = 200/200 and guarded SAFE successes = 200/200. Paired contingency: n11 = 200 (SAFE in both arms), n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Estimated paired SAFE‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10000 resamples, seed = 1729). These numerical outputs are identical to archived analysis artifacts (analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv).

Representative diagnostics. Representative scoring JSONs show identical shared_initial_candidate content for baseline and guarded episodes and validator traces with violation_count = 0 and valid = true. repair_provider_trace fields are null in confirmatory scoring JSONs, confirming that the guarded arm performed only validation and did not modify candidates. The exploratory reserve was not consumed, so no ROC or refusal‑rate estimates were obtained prior to confirmatory execution.

Statistical interpretation. McNemar’s test and paired bootstrap CI rely on discordant pairs (n10, n01). The absence of discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0) yields a degenerate p = 1.0 and CI at zero: the inferential machinery is non‑informative for the preregistered causal estimand under the executed semantics. This degeneracy does not imply verifier effectiveness; it indicates the run lacked arm‑level variation needed to attribute differences to the validator.
sections.discussion:
Why the confirmatory test was uninformative. The degenerate contingency arises from the conjunction of three archived facts: (1) executed generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate (one LLM call per task shared across arms), (2) deterministic_netops_validator_v5 labeled every sampled candidate as valid (baseline SAFE = 200/200), and (3) no repairs were applied (repair_provider_trace null). Under these conditions, neither arm could produce a different candidate to generate discordance; therefore the paired causal contrast could not be evaluated despite meeting the preregistered sample size.

Design implications and artifact‑grounded recommendations. All recommendations follow directly from preregistration and execution artifacts:
- Independent per‑arm generation: to test the causal effect of adding validation, use independent per‑arm draws so each arm can produce different candidates; for N=200 this requires ≈400 model calls (preregistered maximum_model_calls) instead of the 200 executed. The model_call arithmetic is explicit in the execution manifest.
- Calibrate adversarial transforms using the preregistered exploratory reserve (up to 50 tasks) until the baseline unsafe rate matches power assumptions; archive tuning runs and freeze the transform parameters before confirmatory execution.
- If repairs are part of the guarded pipeline, instrument and archive repair_provider_trace artifacts and quantify UNSAFE→SAFE conversions and any introduced violations; in our run repairs were null, so repairs could not generate discordance.
- Pilot check: run a small preregistered pilot and inspect contingency counts; if the pilot shows a ceiling/floor effect (no discordance), switch to a preregistered contingency‑preserving path (enable independent draws or strengthen adversarial injections) before the main confirmatory test.

Alternative estimands when budgets constrain independent draws. If independent per‑arm generation is infeasible, adopt estimands testable under shared semantics: (a) absolute unsafe‑proposal rate of the LLM baseline with CIs; (b) guarded pipeline refusal rate and post‑repair SAFE rate (requires repair execution); or (c) diagnostic ROC estimation using an injected ground truth set (requires exploratory reserve). These alternatives were preregistered as secondary or exploratory estimands and preserve inferential validity under constrained budgets.

Threats to validity and operational caveats. Construct validity: tasks were synthetic, limited to admin/mtu/vlan fields and single‑AS topologies; validator completeness relative to real production failure modes is limited. External validity: single model (gpt‑5‑mini) and synthetic scope preclude generalization to multi‑vendor production networks. Conclusion validity: the confirmatory power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline unsafe rate (~10–15%); that assumption failed here and invalidated power guarantees. Operational implication: teams must weigh the extra model call cost for independent draws against the operational risk of proceeding with insufficiently informative tests.

Reproducibility. All numerical summaries, contingency tables, representative scoring JSONs, execution manifest, and analysis logs are archived in the supplied bundle and permit deterministic replay of the executed, non‑informative outcome. Key artifacts enabling replay are execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, execution/execution_manifest.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, and analysis/condition_summary.csv (compactly referenced rather than enumerated in full throughout the text). Investigators should consult these artifacts before attempting repeats or production extrapolation.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully archived preregistered paired experiment comparing gpt-5-mini baseline generation and a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms yielded zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0]). Because identical per‑pair generations were used and the baseline unsafe rate was 0%, the preregistered causal hypothesis was not testable in this run. The scientific contribution is methodological and reproducibility‑centred: (1) a complete deterministic preregistered run with archived artifacts permitting exact replay; (2) an artifact‑grounded diagnosis of why this execution was non‑informative for verifier efficacy; and (3) concrete, archive‑supported recommendations (independent per‑arm generation budgeting, adversarial calibration, exploratory ROC estimation, and pilot checks) to ensure informative repeats. Future confirmatory runs should adopt these recommendations and archive pilot and tuning steps to preserve preregistered testability assumptions.

limitations: Synthetic tasks and scope: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 and limited to single‑AS, multi‑device setups; results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Generation semantics: the executed run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical per‑pair generations and creating a ceiling effect when shared candidates were valid.

Adversarial strength: the preregistered adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger adversarial cases or explicit injected unsafe examples are required to measure verifier effect.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no multi‑model generality is claimed.

Verifier completeness: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 ran deterministically in synthetic sandboxed states; external validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs remain unquantified at scale.
